title: How much of the SAE dictionary lies in the J-space
takeaway: Across a million-feature sparse autoencoder dictionary, the distribution of J-lens kurtosis is heavy-tailed: most features are read diffusely by the lens, and only a thin tail is read sharply. Counting by layer, the fraction of features that clear a kurtosis threshold is near zero in the early layers, rises at the workspace boundary, and peaks at roughly 15% of the dictionary once motor features are excluded.
walkthrough:
The figure asks how much of a model's learned feature inventory sits inside the [[j-space]], using a [[sparse-autoencoder]] as the inventory. An SAE decomposes the [[residual-stream]] into a large dictionary of feature directions, each with a decoder vector.

The measurement runs each decoder direction through the [[jacobian-lens]], which returns one score per vocabulary token. The sharpness of that score distribution is the feature's [[lens-kurtosis]], written $\kappa$. High $\kappa$ means the direction loads onto a few [[j-lens-vector]]s. Low $\kappa$ means it spreads thinly over the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]], and the feature is outside the workspace.

The left panel is the distribution of $\kappa$ over the roughly one million features of the layer-50 SAE. It is plotted against a covariance-matched random baseline: random directions sharing the second-order geometry of the real decoders. The match matters because the residual stream is anisotropic on its own, so an unmatched baseline would credit the features with sharpness that the geometry already supplies. The real distribution is heavy-tailed. The bulk of features sit at low $\kappa$, and a long tail is read sharply.

The middle panel changes the unit from features to layers. Depth runs along the horizontal axis in the paper's percentage convention ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]); the vertical axis is the fraction of that layer's dictionary whose $\kappa$ clears a threshold set by the baseline. Two curves are drawn, one counting every high-$\kappa$ feature and one excluding [[motor-features]] — features that fire just before, and push for, a specific output token. Motor features also have high $\kappa$, so excluding them isolates [[workspace-features]].

The fraction starts to rise at the workspace boundary, near layer 38, and peaks around 15% of the dictionary after the motor exclusion.

The right panel repeats the middle one with each feature weighted by its activation $L_0$ and by its activation $L_1$. The paper reads this as J-space features activating more strongly than average while firing less often, at least across the second half of the workspace range, which it calls consistent with all-or-nothing [[ignition]].

The paper hedges the whole analysis: SAE features do not necessarily carve the representation space at its joints, and high $\kappa$ is necessary but not sufficient for a feature to be a workspace feature.

terms.definition: An unsupervised dictionary-learning method that rewrites an activation as a sparse sum of feature directions, each meant to correspond to one sometimes-interpretable property of the input or context. Here it supplies the population of directions being scored.
The residual-stream vector an SAE writes back when one of its features is active. It is the object projected through the J-lens in every panel of this figure.

The region of activation space reachable as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors — the paper's candidate global workspace. A feature is judged to be "in" it by how sharply the lens reads its decoder direction.

The paper's technique that assigns each vocabulary token a residual-stream direction encoding the model's disposition to say that token. Projecting a direction through it yields a score over the whole vocabulary.
One vector per vocabulary token per layer, the unit of the J-space. A feature counts as J-space-aligned when its direction is concentrated on a small set of these rather than spread over all of them.
The statistic on the left panel's horizontal axis: how sharply peaked a feature's J-lens score distribution over the vocabulary is. The paper uses excess kurtosis, measured relative to a Gaussian.
Kurtosis measured relative to a Gaussian, so that a Gaussian scores 0 rather than 3. All κ values quoted in this section are excess values.

The comparison distribution in the left panel: random directions drawn to share the covariance structure of the real SAE decoders. It removes the sharpness that the residual stream's own anisotropy would produce for any direction at all.
The depth at which the SAE used in the left panel was trained, given on the paper's 0-100 depth scale. It sits inside the workspace band rather than at either end.

The cutoff used in the middle and right panels: a feature is counted as J-space-aligned when its κ exceeds what the covariance-matched random baseline produces. It turns the continuous left-panel distribution into a yes-or-no count.
The vertical axis of the middle and right panels: the share of that layer's SAE dictionary whose κ clears the threshold. It is a proportion of the dictionary, not of the model's activation.
SAE features that activate immediately before a specific token and promote its utterance. They also have high κ, so the figure plots the fraction both with and without them.

High-κ features that name an abstract concept and fire when that concept is invoked, without the model being about to say the word. These are what the middle panel's motor-excluded curve is meant to count.
The bulk of the dictionary, filling the left panel's mode: syntactic and surface-level bookkeeping features whose lens readouts bear no relation to their apparent meaning.
Depth in the middle and right panels, reported on the paper's rescaled 0-100 index over 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, so a layer number reads as a percentage of depth.
The depth, near layer 38 in this model, at which the paper's other statistics say the J-space starts carrying meaningful content. The middle panel's rise begins there.

The weighting used in one right-panel curve: how often a feature is active across data. Weighting the fraction by L0 asks what share of firing events, rather than of dictionary entries, is J-space-aligned.
The weighting used in the other right-panel curve: the summed magnitude of a feature's activations. Weighting by L1 asks what share of total activation mass is J-space-aligned.

In global workspace theory, the all-or-nothing amplification by which one item enters the workspace. The paper reads strong-but-infrequent activation of J-space features as consistent with such dynamics.

numbers.meaning: The layer whose SAE supplies the left panel's kurtosis distribution, on the paper's 0-100 depth index. It lies inside the workspace band, which the paper places at roughly layers 38 to 92, so it is a layer where J-space content is expected to exist.
The number of features in that layer-50 SAE dictionary. It is the sample size behind the left panel's histogram, and the denominator for the fractions in the other two panels.

The peak fraction of the dictionary that clears the kurtosis threshold, once motor features are excluded. The paper reports this as the high point of the middle panel's motor-excluded curve, so the great majority of features remain outside the J-space at every depth.

The workspace onset the paper locates elsewhere from four lens-derived statistics. The middle panel's fraction begins to rise here, which is why the paper describes the rise as starting at the workspace boundary rather than at an arbitrary depth.

The end of the workspace band, where J-lens readouts turn into predictions of the imminent output. Motor features dominate near this depth, which is what the motor-excluded curve in the middle panel is designed to strip out.

The criterion for labelling a feature "motor": over the feature's strongest activations, the actual next token appears among its 10 most strongly expressed lens tokens more than 10% of the time. Only features meeting this test are removed from the second middle-panel curve.
The excess kurtosis of a Gaussian, and so the origin of the left panel's scale. Values near 0 mean a feature's lens readout is no more peaked than chance.

The lens-kurtosis of the "numeric constraints and ranges" feature discussed alongside this figure, and its position in this same distribution. It fixes where the left panel's far tail begins: a κ near 21 is a one-in-a-thousand feature.

The lens-kurtosis of three example bookkeeping features — a decrementing loop variable, the first digit of a citation page range, and a markdown section header. They sit in the left panel's bulk, and none of their top lens tokens relates to the feature's apparent meaning.

numbers.value: second half of the workspace range
numbers.meaning: The depth span over which the paper reports the L0-weighted fraction falling below the unweighted one — that is, where J-space features fire less often than average. The paper limits the claim to this span rather than to the workspace band as a whole.
